question: A 72-year-old male visits his gastroenterologist for a check-up one year following resection of a 2-cm malignant lesion in his sigmoid colon. Serum levels of which of the following can be used in this patient to test for cancer recurrence?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Carcinoembryonic antigen" -> "marker for colorectal cancer" -> "used to monitor recurrence" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Alpha-fetoprotein" -> "marker for liver cancer" -> "not typically used for colorectal cancer" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Cancer antigen 125 (CA-125)" -> "marker for ovarian cancer" -> "not typically used for colorectal cancer" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Gamma glutamyl transferase" -> "liver enzyme" -> "not a specific cancer marker" -> 10%
CHAIN: "CA-19-9 tumor marker" -> "marker for pancreatic cancer" -> "sometimes elevated in colorectal cancer" -> 30%
enhanced_information: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a well-established marker for colorectal cancer and is commonly used to monitor for recurrence after treatment. This aligns with the consensus that CEA is the most appropriate serum marker for detecting recurrence in a patient with a history of colorectal cancer. Alpha-fetoprotein is primarily a marker for liver cancer and is not used for colorectal cancer. Cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) is associated with ovarian cancer and not relevant for colorectal cancer. Gamma glutamyl transferase is a liver enzyme and not a specific marker for any cancer type. CA-19-9 is a marker for pancreatic cancer and may sometimes be elevated in colorectal cancer, but it is not the primary marker for monitoring recurrence in colorectal cancer. Therefore, the best option for monitoring cancer recurrence in this patient is carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).
analysis: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a well-established tumor marker used in the follow-up of patients with colorectal cancer. It is commonly used to monitor for recurrence after surgical resection of colorectal cancer. The other options, such as alpha-fetoprotein, CA-125, gamma glutamyl transferase, and CA-19-9, are associated with other types of cancers or conditions and are not typically used for monitoring colorectal cancer recurrence.
